countries.name: Albania
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2015)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 8.2% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 12.5% of households
* Most at risk: lower-income households, older people and households with children
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines and inpatient care on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households

**Unmet need (2023)**

* Health care: 10.3% of people
* Dental care: 12.5% of people

[Albania page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Albania)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: The Mandatory Health Insurance Fund (MHIF) only covers about two thirds of the population on average and only about half of those in the poorest fifth of the population. People not covered by the MHIF tend to be informal workers, people with low incomes, those from minority communities (Roma and Egyptian people) and people living in deprived areas. Non-covered people are only entitled to publicly financed emergency care, an annual basic screening and counselling health check-up (since 2015 and for people aged 35-70 years only) and primary care visits (since 2017). They also face difficulties in using the e-Albania portal, which limits their access to health care.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Although the publicly financed benefits package is relatively comprehensive, the range of covered medicines remains low by European standards, there is no entitlement to dental care for adults and entitlement to dental care for children is limited. Informal payments are widespread for services and supplies that should be available free of charge, mainly in inpatient care.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges in the form of percentage co-payments are applied to outpatient prescribed medicines and diagnostic tests and other paramedical services (e.g. physiotherapy, counselling). Protection from co-payments is weak: there is no overall cap on co-payments and, although exemptions are available for some groups of people and some services, they do not target people with low incomes. There are no formal user charges for inpatient medicines, but people report having to purchase their own medicines in hospitals. The complexity of co-payment policy lowers transparency and undermines public trust in the health system.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a very small supplementary role in the health system, covering access to health care in private facilities (mainly hospitals). In 2020 it accounted for 0% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: De-link entitlement to publicly financed health services from payment of contributions for the whole population
recommendations.text: Albania should start by extending Mandatory Health Insurance Fund (MHIF) benefits to the whole population so that access no longer depends on payment of contributions. Linking entitlement to payment of MHIF contributions is particularly challenging given Albania’s large informal sector.

recommendations.title: Simplify the complex design of user charges and strengthen protection mechanisms
recommendations.text: User charges are complex and particularly heavy for outpatient prescribed medicines. Co-payment policy should be re-designed in the following ways: replace percentage co-payments with low, fixed co-payments; exempt households with low incomes from all co-payments; introduce an annual income-related cap covering all co-payments.

recommendations.title: Strengthen medicines policy
recommendations.text: Attention should be paid to the way in which medicines are selected for coverage and to ensuring that physicians, pharmacists and people are able to prescribe, dispense and use the cheapest alternatives.

recommendations.title: Increase public spending on health and use resources to meet equity and efficiency goals
recommendations.text: Strengthening financial protection will require additional public spending on health and a greater focus on improving affordable access to health care for households with low incomes.

countries.name: Andorra
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2024)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 1.6% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 3.8% of households
* Main drivers: dental care on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need**

Internationally comparable data on unmet need are not available for Andorra

[Andorra page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Andorra)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text:
The basis for entitlement to publicly financed health care is payment of mandatory health contributions. As a result around 2% of the population is not covered by the Andorran Social Security Office (Caixa Andorrana de Seguretat Social or CASS). However, most of these people have some form of coverage through their home-country health system (e.g. teachers from France and Spain) or VHI. Only 0.1% of the population has no form of coverage at all.

Adult undocumented migrants are entitled to emergency care only, which they have to pay for fully out of pocket. If they are accredited as having a low income, the out-of-pocket payments can be waived. The Minister of Social Affairs can provide full entitlement (the same as residents) to people granted health protection.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Although the publicly financed benefits package is comprehensive, access can be limited by the widespread use of retrospective reimbursement (applied to most outpatient care for most people) and staff shortages and waiting times for some specialist care.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to all types of health care in the form of percentage co-payments. There is also reference pricing for outpatient prescribed medicines and balance billing for medical products. Although there are exemptions in place for people with low incomes and for some chronic conditions, there is no cap on co-payments. A large share of the population (around 73% in 2023) has VHI covering co-payments for publicly financed health care.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays mainly a complementary (user charges) role, covering user charges for covered care. It plays a minor substitutive role providing coverage for ‘passive residents’ (foreign residents with certain economic conditions and no working permit e.g. foreign retired people) who are required to purchase VHI. In 2023 73% of the population had complementary VHI covering user charges (co-payments). In 2023 it accounted for 18.1% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

countries.name: Armenia
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2021)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 7.9% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 17.1% of households
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines on average and especially for low-income households


**Unmet need**

Internationally comparable data on unmet need are not available for Armenia

[Armenia page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Armenia)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Entitlement to publicly financed health care is based on residence, but only half of the population has access to the full range of publicly financed health care. All residents and refugees are entitled to outpatient care (including primary care and some specialist visits but excluding dental care) and some inpatient care. Only some residents and refugees (military staff, civil servants or other social package beneficiaries, people who have cancer or TB or who require intensive care) and asylum seekers are entitled to other publicly financed health care.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Publicly financed coverage of inpatient care is limited for half of the population. Coverage of outpatient prescribed medicines, medical products, diagnostic tests and dental care is limited for the whole population. Covered people tend to face long waiting times for inpatient care and there are no policies to reduce waits. Informal payments are high, especially for inpatient care. There is a shortage of physicians outside Yerevan. Public spending on health is very low.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Co-payments are applied to publicly financed outpatient prescribed medicines, diagnostic tests, dental care treatment and inpatient care for some groups of people, often in the form of percentage co-payments. Exemptions from co-payments are complex and are not yet applied automatically. There is no overall cap on co-payments.

countries.name: Austria
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2020)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 1.9% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 4.2% of households
* Main drivers: dental care and outpatient care on average; outpatient medicines, dental care and medical products for low-income households

**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 1% of people
* Dental care: 1.1% of people

[Austria page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Austria)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: A small share of the population (0.01–0.02% depending on the data source) lacks social health insurance (SHI) scheme coverage. Undocumented migrants are not entitled to SHI coverage. Because entitlement to SHI benefits is based on payment of contributions, some people without stable employment, people with serious mental health problems, homeless people and some unemployed people (women in particular) also lack coverage. More recent administrative data suggest that people lacking SHI coverage include unregistered asylum seekers and students too old to be covered as dependants.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Waiting times for elective treatment in public hospitals and related issues with informal payments and incentives to prioritise people with VHI. Some variation in benefits across social health insurance funds. Increasing shortages of medicines, particularly for antimicrobial substances. A lack of contracted psychotherapists and midwives.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Co-payment policy varies across social health insurance schemes and funds for outpatient visits, dental care and medical products and across regions for inpatient care. People with low incomes and people with chronic conditions are not systematically exempt from co-payments. There is variation in the cap on co-payments for medical products and no overall cap on co-payments.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI mainly offers access to private physicians, enhanced amenities in hospital and faster access to treatment. It also plays a small complementary role, providing access to some services that are not covered by the social health insurance scheme. For a very small share of the population, VHI plays a substitutive role for people who opt out of the SHI scheme. In 2022 it accounted for 4.6% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
countries.summary:
__At present, we do not have numbers on financial hardship for Azerbaijan. See Policy explorer for information on coverage policy.__

[Policy explorer](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/policy-explorer?country=ST86paYjRHP)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: There is little information about gaps in coverage. Migrants and refugees are formally entitled to all publicly financed health care but may face administrative barriers to accessing services. Undocumented migrants and asylum seekers are entitled to emergency care only.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage of outpatient medicines is extremely limited: medicines are only publicly financed through state vertical programmes covering a handful of conditions (oncology, thalassemia, preventive services for children, vaccination, haemophilia, diabetes, tuberculosis, renal failure and HIV/AIDS). Dental care is not covered. People face barriers to accessing care in rural areas due to poor health infrastructure and workforce shortages. Informal payments are widespread.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are currently applied to diagnostic tests and to specialist care without referral. There are no exemptions from co-payments and there is no cap on co-payments. New user charges are to be introduced in 2025.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a supplementary role, providing access to private health care facilities, and a complementary (services) role, granting access to outpatient medicines and dental care. It accounted for 2.4% of current spending on health in 2021. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

countries.name: Belgium
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2020)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 1.1% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 5.2% of households
* Most at risk: lower-income households, unemployed people, inactive people and people with a lower level of education
* Main drivers: medical products on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households

**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 0.9% of people
* Dental care: 3.2% of people

[Belgium page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Belgium)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text:
In 2022 about 1% of the population was not covered (uninsured), rising to 1.3% in Brussels and 2% among younger adults (20–39 years).

Lack of access to social health insurance coverage for asylum seekers, undocumented migrants, posted workers (people sent by their employer to carry out a service in another EU Member State on a temporary basis), homeless people and people who cannot afford to pay contributions.

People whose social contributions are not automatically collected face complex coverage rules."

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text:
Social health insurance (SHI) coverage of dental care and medical products (e.g. hearing aids and optical care such as glasses and contact lenses) is limited and SHI does not cover over-the-counter medicines.

Although mandatory complementary health insurance (CHI) provided by sickness funds covers services like orthodontics and optical care (glasses and contact lenses), it is financed through flat-rate contributions, which are regressive.

Benefits in kind (third-party payment) do not automatically apply to all outpatient care, only to inpatient care and outpatient medicines.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text:
Complex co-payments are applied to almost all health services, including primary care visits.
There are very few exemptions from co-payments (e.g. for dental care for children < 19 and general practitioner and outpatient specialist care for children and young adults < 25 eligible for ‘increased reimbursement’ and with a global medical record) and no general exemption for people with low incomes.
Reduced co-payments are not automatically granted to low-income households and there are major gaps in take-up.
Balance billing is widespread in hospitals (‘fee supplements’) and in outpatient care.
Co-payment protection mechanisms do not apply to balance billing.
Most outpatient care is subject to retrospective reimbursement.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a mixed complementary and supplementary role. It initially focused on offering subscribers a fixed payment a day in hospital, but over time coverage has been extended to co-payments (and other user charges) for hospital stays to account for increases in balance billing (fee supplements). VHI can also cover dental care and ambulatory services, including balance billing and other co-payments, but this part of the market is relatively small. Although VHI is estimated to cover quite a large share of the population, richer households are much more likely to be covered than households with lower incomes. In 2022 it accounted for 4.7% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Ensure the social health insurance (SHI) scheme covers the whole population
recommendations.text: The Government should find ways to ensure that the whole population is covered.

recommendations.title: Continue to strengthen co-payment policy so that it is better able to protect households with low incomes
recommendations.text:
Grant automatic entitlement to everyone eligible for reduced co-payments (increased reimbursement) to eliminate administrative barriers to take-up.
\
\
Find a way to reduce co-payments for households with low incomes – for example, by exempting them from co-payments, further lowering the annual cap on co-payments (maximum billing [maximumfactuur-maximum a facturer], MAF) for them or introducing an additional lower cap targeted at households with very low incomes.
\
\
Raise awareness of the cap by informing people about it at the beginning of each year instead of waiting until they cross the spending threshold.
\
\
Extend the cap to user charges for prescribed non-covered medicines and long-term psychiatric care.

recommendations.title: Abolish retrospective reimbursement for all health services covered by the SHI scheme
recommendations.text: This includes abolishing all up-front payment of co-payments above the cap (MAF).

recommendations.title: Continue to limit balance billing in outpatient and inpatient care
recommendations.text: Further regulate and reform the way in which hospitals are financed. Increase the share of ‘conventioned’ practitioners who apply the official tariff and abolish partial ‘conventioning’.

recommendations.title: Reduce out-of-pocket payments for medical products
recommendations.text: Further strengthen regulation of the price of non-covered medical products such as hearing aids, glasses and contact lenses.

countries.name: Bulgaria
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2018)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 8% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 19.2% of households
* Most at risk: lower-income households, older people and people in rural areas
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines on average and especially for low-income households

**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 1% of people
* Dental care: 2% of people

[Bulgaria page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Bulgaria)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: About 11% of the population was estimated to lack coverage by the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) in 2022. A significant share of people not covered by the NHIF includes those who are permanently unemployed and cannot afford to pay contributions. Undocumented migrants are not entitled to be covered by the NHIF.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Limited coverage of outpatient medicines, medical products, dental care, long-term nursing care and long-term rehabilitation.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to almost all health care. Percentage co-payments are applied to outpatient medicines. There are no exemptions from co-payments for outpatient medicines and many people with low incomes are not exempt from other user charges. There is no cap on user charges for outpatient care, including outpatient medicines and medical products.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a minor complementary role, covering services that are not covered by the NHIF, and a supplementary role offering faster access to treatment and free choice of physician or clinical team in hospital. In 2022 it accounted for less than 1% of current spending on health and covered around 10% of the population in 2022. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Ensure the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) covers the whole population
recommendations.text: The Government can stop penalizing people who do not pay mandatory contributions by restricting access to health care. Instead, it can allow the tax agency to address non-payment of mandatory contributions in the same way the tax agency addresses non-payment of other taxes.

recommendations.title: Strengthen co-payment policy
recommendations.text: Replace percentage co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines with low, fixed co-payments; exempt households with low incomes and people with chronic conditions from all co-payments; and introduce an annual income-based cap on all co-payments.

recommendations.title: Improve medicines policy
recommendations.text: Improve the way in which the NHIF purchases outpatient medicines. Continue to reduce medicine prices. Make sure health care providers and pharmacies have incentives to prescribe and dispense the cheapest alternatives.

recommendations.title: Increase public spending on health and use resources to meet equity and efficiency goals
recommendations.text: Spending should be targeted carefully to increase efficiency throughout the health system and to reduce financial hardship and unmet need for households with low incomes.

countries.recommendationsSource: Source: [‘Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in Bulgaria’ (2020)](https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/349200).

countries.name: Croatia
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2019)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 1.9% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 3.6% of households
* Main drivers: dental care and outpatient medicines on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 1.3% of people
* Dental care: 0.5% of people

[Croatia page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Croatia)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Undocumented migrants, asylum seekers and non-resident foreigners from countries outside the European Union are not entitled to mandatory health insurance benefits.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Waiting times are an issue, but there are no waiting time guarantees in place. Informal payments play a small role in the health system.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to all health services except emergency care. People with low incomes are not exempt from co-payments but can apply for free complementary VHI covering co-payments. The cap on co-payments is set at a high level and only applies per episode of care, not over time. It does not apply to co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: Around 80% of the population has complementary VHI covering co-payments. This type of VHI is mainly supplied by the Croatian Institute of Health Insurance (HZZO) but also by private insurers. A quarter of those with complementary VHI supplied by the HZZO benefit from free access to VHI: the Government pays premiums for students, people with low incomes, people with severe disabilities and blood and organ donors. Despite this subsidy, households in the poorest fifth of the population spend a higher share of their budget on VHI than those in the richest fifth. VHI also plays a minor supplementary role, giving 8% of the population access to private providers, mainly for diagnostic services. In 2020 VHI accounted for 5.3% of current spending on health.

recommendations.title: Improve access to complementary VHI for households with low incomes
recommendations.text: Raising the income threshold for eligibility for free complementary VHI would ensure that all households in the poorest fifth of the population are able to benefit. This would also help to address the regressivity of VHI premiums.

recommendations.title: Strengthen protection from co-payments through better design
recommendations.text: This can be done by extending the current list of exemptions from co-payments to include low-income households and by improving the cap on co-payments – for example, by applying it to all co-payments and ensuring it provides protection over time rather than per episode of care.

recommendations.title: Improve the affordability of non-covered medicines
recommendations.text: The lack of price regulation for non-covered medicines, including over-the-counter medicines, may be an issue, especially since medicines account for the bulk of out-of-pocket payments and catastrophic spending on health.

countries.recommendationsSource: Source: [‘Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in Croatia’ (2018)](https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/329441).

countries.name: Cyprus
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2015)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 1.8% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 5% of households
* Most at risk: lower-income households, older people and people who are publicly covered and do not have voluntary health insurance
* Main drivers: diagnostic tests and inpatient care on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households

**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 0.1% of people
* Dental care: 1.8% of people

[Cyprus page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Cyprus)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Undocumented migrants and students from countries outside the European Union are not covered by the General Health System (GHS). Non-Cypriot citizens, particularly those from outside the European Union, may face administrative barriers to accessing the GHS because of the requirement to register with the Civil Registry and Migration Department.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage is limited for long-term care, dental care, palliative care and rehabilitation and glasses, contact lenses and hearing aids are excluded from coverage. Waiting times are an issue for some specialist consultations.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to most health care. Emergency care is subject to co-payments with some exemptions. People with low incomes are exempt from some co-payments. There is an annual cap on co-payments per person and the cap is set at a lower, more protective level for people receiving the Guaranteed Minimum Income, pensioners with low incomes and children and young people (0–21 years).

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a complementary (services mostly), supplementary and substitutive (very minor) role. In 2022 it accounted for 3.2% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

countries.name: Czechia
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2023)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 3% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 5.7% of households
* Main drivers: dental care and outpatient medicines on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 0.3% of people
* Dental care: 1% of people

[Czechia page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Czechia)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Access to publicly financed health care, including social health insurance (SHI) benefits, is based on permanent residence, so all permanent residents are covered. The people most likely to lack SHI coverage are undocumented migrants, who are not entitled to any publicly financed health care.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage of corrective lenses is limited for adults and although dental care is fully covered, it is limited in terms of scope and materials and most dentists are not willing to offer covered procedures or use covered materials. Specialist health care is less accessible outside large cities and there is a shortage of pharmacies and dentists in border areas. Waiting times are an issue in paediatric care. Waiting time targets are in place but are not guaranteed because they are not systematically monitored. Informal payments are not systematically monitored either but international data sources suggest they are higher in Czechia than in most EU countries and typically occur in maternity care to shorten waiting times or see a specific doctor.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to outpatient emergency care (fixed co-payments) and outpatient prescribed medicines and medical products (reference pricing). People with low incomes are exempt from co-payments for emergency care. There are no exemptions from other co-payments but there is an annual cap on some co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines, which is lower (more protective) for children, older people and people with disabilities. There is no cap on all co-payments. Although extra billing is not permitted, some health care providers charge people for non-clinical services (e.g. scheduling appointments at specific times or sending people text message reminders), particularly in larger cities.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a minor substitutive role, covering non-EU nationals who are obliged to buy private health insurance. In 2023 VHI accounted for 0.1% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Build on recent efforts to reduce the “avoidable co-payments” caused by reference pricing for outpatient prescribed medicines
recommendations.text: This can be done by ensuring that the fully covered medicine in each reference group is available in pharmacies; waiving reference pricing when the fully covered medicine is not available at the local pharmacy; exempting people with low incomes from co-payments currently eligible for the cap or extending the lowest cap (CZK 500) to people with low incomes; finding other ways to link the cap on co-payments to income; closely monitoring “avoidable co-payments” and their causes; further reducing the VAT rate for covered medicines; and improving access to pharmacies in underserved areas.

recommendations.title: Reduce out-of-pocket payments for dental care
recommendations.text: This can be achieved by requiring dental care providers to offer covered services and materials; expanding the coverage of dental care, including the use of higher-quality materials; and improving access to dental care in underserved areas.

recommendations.title: Expand coverage of medical products, especially for people with low incomes
Reduce out-of-pocket payments for outpatient visits
recommendations.text: This can be done by removing administrative barriers to the exemption from co-payments for emergency care or abolish this co-payment since it is unlikely to be addressing the root cause of inappropriate use of emergency care; enforcing laws prohibiting extra billing; and taking steps to systematically monitor and address long waiting times and informal payments, which reduce transparency and are likely to be particularly detrimental for people with low incomes.

recommendations.title: Address administrative and language barriers that hinder asylum seekers and migrants from accessing entitlements and expand access to publicly financed health care for undocumented migrants
Ensure that public spending on health is able to meet equity and efficiency goals, now and in the future
recommendations.text: Public spending on health should be carefully targeted to reduce financial hardship and unmet need for households with low incomes. The Government can take steps to broaden the SHI scheme’s revenue base is broad so that it will generate sufficient funding as the population ages.

countries.recommendationsSource:
Source: [‘Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in Czechia’ (2025)](https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/381966).

See the coverage policy checklist for country examples of good practice in improving financial protection.

countries.name: Denmark
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2015)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 1.8% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 2.6% of households
* Main drivers: medical products on average; outpatient medicines and dental care for low-income households


**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 3.1% of people
* Dental care: 7.5% of people

[Denmark page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Denmark)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Because the basis for entitlement is residence most of the population is covered. However, people without a residence permit (including undocumented migrants and refugees who are not registered in the National Register) are not entitled to the full range of publicly financed health care and can only access emergency care. Although they are required to pay the full price of any care they receive out of pocket, in practice the regional Government can exempt people with low incomes who are unable to pay. Asylum seekers and victims of human trafficking are entitled to a limited set of health services provided in asylum centres or crisis centres. Administrative barriers may delay access to health care for asylum seekers due to the lengthy residence application and processing time (an average wait of 240 days for asylum seekers and 35 days for Ukrainian refugees in 2023).

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Medical products, including hearing aids and glasses, are not covered. Coverage of physiotherapy, chiropractic care and outpatient visits to psychologists is limited. Dental care is only free for people < 20 and assisted reproductive health services are not covered for people > 41. Waiting times are an issue for some elective treatment and psychiatric services. People living in Denmark for more than three years who require language interpreter services when accessing health care are required to pay a fixed co-payment, which can be quite high for some services.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Fixed co-payments are applied to dental care for people > 21. Percentage co-payments apply to outpatient prescribed medicines. Although there are some exempt groups, these are not based on income and people generally require to submit an online application. There is no overall cap on co-payments. Although there is a cap on co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines, it is not linked to income.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a supplementary role offering access to private providers and faster treatment and a complementary role covering services like medical products (glasses and contact lenses) and user charges for outpatient medicines and dental care. It accounted for 2.5% of current spending on health in 2022. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

countries.name: Estonia
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2020)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 2.2% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 7.2% of households
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines on average and especially for low-income households


**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 7.7% of people
* Dental care: 5.5% of people

[Estonia page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Estonia)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: In 2022 about 4% of people were not covered by the Estonian Health Insurance Fund (EHIF), rising to 10% among people aged 20–29 years. Those most likely to lack coverage are working-age people in part-time or unstable work or people working in the informal economy.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: The EHIF does not cover optician services and products (e.g. glasses and contact lenses) or over-the-counter medicines. Coverage of dental care is very limited for adults. There are long waiting times for specialist outpatient visits and elective surgery. There is a shortage of health care professionals in primary and specialist care, especially in remote areas.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: There are extensive percentage co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines and heavy percentage co-payments for some inpatient nursing care. There are no explicit exemptions from co-payments for people with low incomes, no cap on co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines and no overall cap on co-payments. Balance billing takes place for some primary care services. Extra billing is allowed in facilities contracted by the EHIF.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI does not play significant role in filling gaps in coverage. Since 2002 the EHIF has provided substitutive VHI for those not eligible for mandatory EHIF coverage (617 people in 2021). Supplementary and complementary VHI plays a small but growing role, providing faster access to covered services and some services not covered by the EHIF. VHI accounted for 0.3% of current spending on health in 2021 and covered 7% of the working-age population in 2022. The tax subsidies for VHI introduced in 2018 are likely to increase the number of people with VHI and exacerbate inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Change the basis for entitlement to residence
recommendations.text: The gap in population coverage should be closed by changing the basis for entitlement to Estonian Health Insurance Fund (EHIF) benefits to residence.

recommendations.title: Increase and fine-tune benefits to better target those in most need
recommendations.text:
Dental care and other benefits should be increased and fine-tuned so that they are better targeted to help households in most need.

Protection from co-payments should be increased for households with low incomes – for example, by setting a cap for them or exempting them from all co-payments.

recommendations.title: Monitor and reduce co-payments
recommendations.text:
Co-payments should be monitored in a more person-centred way (that is, looking at co-payments across all types of health care financed by the EHIF) and a cap on all co-payments should be introduced – for example, by extending the protection mechanism used for outpatient prescribed medicines and applying it to all services. 

Out-of-pocket payments for long-term health care can be reduced by abolishing percentage co-payments and establishing a cap – ideally one that applies to co-payments for all types of health care. 

Balance billing for primary care services (such as those provided by psychologists, physiotherapists and speech therapists) should be abolished to ensure that access does not depend on ability to pay.

recommendations.title: Continue to improve medicines policy
recommendations.text: Out-of-pocket payments should continue to be reduced for prescribed medicines and medical products by ensuring that health care providers and pharmacies have incentives to prescribe and dispense the cheapest alternatives and through price regulation.

countries.recommendationsSource: Source: [‘Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in Estonia' (2023)](https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/374504).

countries.name: Finland
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2016)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 1.2% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 3.8% of households
* Most at risk: lower-income households and older people
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines, outpatient care and dental care on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households

**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 7.8% of people
* Dental care: 7.5% of people

[Finland page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Finland)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text:
Entitlement to publicly financed health care is based on residence and age, which means all permanent residents and all children < 18 (regardless of legal or coverage status) are automatically covered. However, employed residents also benefit from occupational health care, giving them significantly faster access to primary care than self-employed or unemployed people and people outside the labour force (e.g. children and pensioners).

Adult asylum seekers, undocumented migrants and adults without a municipality of residence lack entitlement to the full range of publicly financed health care. They have access to a limited set of services, often at the discretion of health care professionals, but are required to pay for them out of pocket – although the Government reimburses municipalities for the care of people with low incomes who are unable to pay.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text:
The presence of multiple coverage schemes leads to complexity and variation in benefits across groups of people and exacerbates inequality in access to health care.

Although the publicly financed benefits package is relatively comprehensive, coverage of eye care (glasses or contact lenses) and psychotherapy is limited.

Access to most health care (especially gynaecology and dental care) is hindered by waiting times. There are differences in access and quality for health care financed by the wellbeing services counties and occupational health care, reflecting long waiting times for non-urgent health and dental care in public facilities and a shortage of doctors in public facilities due to lower wages compared to private facilities.

Geographical barriers to access due to distance affect people in the northernmost parts of the country and, in the last decade, the closure of public facilities has increased travel times for people in southern parts of the country.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Co-payments are widely applied, are complex in design and vary substantially across wellbeing services counties (WSCs), especially for home care. All children < 18 are automatically exempt from co-payments for WSC health care, but there are no automatic exemptions based on household income; instead, people with low incomes must apply for social assistance to cover co-payments for WSC health care and co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines unther the National Health Insurance scheme. As a result, take up of social assistance may be low; only 34% of households that reported financial barriers to accessing health care applied for social assistance and only 17% received it. Although there are annual caps on co-payments for health care (outpatient primary, specialist and emergency care), these caps are separate, set at a high level and not linked to household income; in addition, people have to keep track of co-payments themselves to benefit from these caps. Just 7% of the population reach one of the three caps and only 0.2% reach all three caps.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text:
VHI mainly plays a complementary role covering out-of-pocket payments in private facilities and co-payments for publicly financed health care. It also plays a supplementary role providing faster access to treatment in private facilities. People often seek VHI coverage to access specialist care without a referral or to bypass waiting lists in public primary care facilities. VHI covers the use of health care in non-contracted private facilities, mainly to reduce waiting times for non-working people (e.g. children and pensioners) who are unable to benefit from occupational primary care coverage. VHI covers user charges. Take-up of VHI covering user charges is significant, particularly among children: in 2019 12% of adults and 45% of children had VHI.

The share of the population with VHI has increased over time. In 2019 12% of adults and 45% of children had VHI, up from 8% and 37% respectively in 2009. In 2021 it accounted for 1.6% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

countries.name: France
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2017)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 1.5% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 2.1% of households
* Main drivers: outpatient care and diagnostic tests on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 4.1% of people
* Dental care: 7% of people

[France page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/France)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text:
Undocumented migrants are excluded from the SHI scheme but can benefit from free access to health care through the AME scheme if they have been in France for at least three months and have an annual income of less than €10 339 (for a single person in 2025).

People living in France for less than three months can access emergency care only.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Some types of care are less well-covered by the SHI scheme – particularly dental care and medical products such as glasses and hearing aids. General and specialist outpatient care, dental care and care provided by midwives are subject to retrospective reimbursement by the SHI scheme.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text:
User charges are applied to all types of health care, mainly in the form of percentage co-payments.

There is no cap on percentage co-payments or balance and extra billing. Caps on fixed co-payments are not linked to household income.

Balance billing is permitted for some general practitioners and specialists (in Sector 2), dental care and medical products such as optical care (glasses and contact lenses) and hearing aids; it is also permitted for physician services in SHI-contracted private hospitals.

Extra billing is permitted for inpatient care for non-clinical care (e.g. more comfortable accommodation).

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: Private complementary health insurance (CHI) plays a substantial role in the French health system, mainly covering co-payments and balance billing for social health insurance benefits. It is mandatory and subsidized by employers for employees in private companies and free or subsidized by the Government for people with low incomes. As a result, CHI covers around 95% of the population and accounted for 12% of current spending on health in 2024 (WHO, 2026). It does not fully address the problems caused by user charges, however: households with the lowest incomes are the least likely to have any form of CHI and CHI is a highly regressive way of financing the health system. It also involves significant transaction and financial costs for the Government and employers.

recommendations.title: Improve the use of public resources to reduce co-payments, including balance billing
recommendations.text: This can be achieved by exempting CSS beneficiaries and people with chronic conditions from all co-payments so that they no longer need Complementary Health Insurance (CHI); and by introducing an annual cap on all co-payments for the whole population and linking it to household income. Other options to reduce financial uncertainty, increase transparency and enhance access include, for example, limiting balance billing for all types of health care, replacing percentage co-payments with low, fixed co-payments and phasing out retrospective reimbursement.

recommendations.title: Reduce the regressivity of complementary health insurance (CHI)
recommendations.text: This could be achieved by simplifying and automating administrative procedures to prevent households from losing CSS coverage from one year to another; setting monthly contributions at levels that encourage higher take-up among those eligible; reviewing eligibility thresholds to ensure they cover all people at risk of poverty or social exclusion; and linking subsidies for CHI for government and private-sector employees to income so that they are more generous for people with lower incomes.

recommendations.title: Improve coverage of dental care and access for underserved groups
recommendations.text: The Government can also improve the coverage of dental care, to reduce income inequality in unmet need for this type of care.

recommendations.title: Find ways to ensure the whole population is covered
recommendations.text: Access to publicly financed health care for undocumented migrants could be improved by simplifying and automating administrative procedures.

countries.recommendationsSource:
Source: ['Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in France' (2024)](https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/376550).

See the coverage policy checklist for country examples of good practice in improving financial protection.

countries.name: Germany
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2018)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 1% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 2.4% of households
* Main drivers: dental care on average; outpatient medicines and medical products for low-income households


**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 1.2% of people
* Dental care: 1.5% of people

[Germany page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Germany)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text:
The main basis for entitlement is payment of contributions to the social health insurance (SHI) scheme or payment of premiums for substitutive private health insurance (PHI). This can create problems for self-employed people with no or low incomes or for people who cannot afford PHI premiums but are not permitted to return to the SHI scheme (e.g. people with PHI who are > 55 and have not been covered by SHI for the last five years). Those who have stopped paying mandatory contributions or premiums, as well as undocumented migrants, are entitled to a limited range of publicly financed health care only, mainly emergency care. Census data indicate that around 0.07% of the population (about 61 000 people) had no health care coverage at all in 2019 – mainly self-employed people with no earnings, people with low incomes and younger adults.

Refugees and asylum seekers in their first 36 months in Germany need to obtain a health voucher (valid for three months) to access the full range of publicly financed health care, and this may represent an administrative barrier to access.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: The benefits package is relatively comprehensive, but coverage of non-standard dental care and over-the-counter medicines is limited. Although there are some inequalities in waiting time for treatment between people covered by the social health insurance (SHI) scheme and people with substitutive private health insurance (PHI), waiting times are generally not long by international standards.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges in the form of percentage co-payments are applied to outpatient prescribed medicines, medical products and dental care treatment (dentures and selected other treatment) and fixed co-payments are applied to inpatient care. Children < 18 are exempt from all co-payments, but people with low incomes and recipients of social welfare are only exempt from co-payments for covered dental care treatment. Although there is an income-based cap on all co-payments, which is lower for people with chronic conditions, people must apply to benefit from it, potentially limiting take-up.

countries.name: Greece
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2023)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 3.4% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 9.5% of households
* Main drivers: inpatient care and outpatient medicines on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 12.1% of people
* Dental care: 12.9% of people

[Greece page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Greece)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Non-covered legal residents can only access health care in public facilities. Undocumented migrants only have access to emergency care for the treatment of life-threatening conditions and communicable diseases. Administrative barriers such as delays in access to an alien health care card (KYPA) or provisional social security number (PAAYPA) can hinder access to entitlements for undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. Most Roma lack any form of coverage or face barriers to access due to the lack of birth registration, identity cards and other documents. They also lack targeted information campaigns and may face negative attitudes from health professionals.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage of dental care is limited, particularly for adults. Caps on service volumes limit access to outpatient care, including outpatient prescribed medicines and diagnostic tests. Although waiting times are an issue, there are no waiting time guarantees. Informal payments are widespread, particularly in public hospitals.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to most types of outpatient care, as well as to inpatient care provided in private facilities contracted by EOPPY. Many user charges were increased during the economic crisis. There are not many exemptions targeting people with low incomes. There is no cap on co-payments.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI mainly plays a supplementary role, offering people faster access to treatment and greater choice of provider. It is generally sold in combination with life insurance or private pension schemes and typically covers expenses in private facilities, including facilities owned by insurance companies. In 2021 it accounted for 4.2% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Extend the benefits covered by the National Organization for the Provision of Health Services (EOPYY) to all residents to reduce inequalities in access to health care
recommendations.text: Basing entitlement to EOPYY benefits on employment and payment of mandatory contributions undermines health system resilience to shocks. Although the law introduced in 2016 improved access for many people, it perpetuated a two-tier system in which those not covered by EOPYY rely on health care in public facilities and face greater barriers to access due to longer waiting times and shortages of staff and equipment. The two-tier system is also unfair because many taxpayers are not entitled to EOPYY benefits even though they contribute to the financing of EOPYY through the government budget; this includes (but is not limited to) people who have paid contributions to EOPYY (or its predecessors) while working but are no longer eligible for EOPYY benefits due to long-term unemployment. These challenges can be addressed by changing the basis for entitlement to EOPYY benefits from payment of contributions to residence, which would not require any fundamental change in the way EOPYY is financed. Rather, it would mean that: all residents would be entitled to the same health care benefits; and non-payment of contributions would be treated in the same way as non-payment of other taxes (for example, through fines rather than by denying access to services).

recommendations.title: Simplify and strengthen the design of co-payments, particularly for outpatient medicines and other forms of outpatient care
recommendations.text: International evidence and experience show that this can be done by extending exemptions from all co-payments (including the avoidable copayments caused by internal reference pricing) to more households with low incomes; introducing an income-based cap on all co-payments; replacing percentage co-payments with low, fixed co-payments; and applying protection mechanisms automatically, with the help of digital tools, to simplify access and maximize take up.

recommendations.title: Continue to improve financial protection for people who need outpatient medicines and other forms of outpatient care
recommendations.text: In addition to strengthening protection from co-payments, this can be achieved by ensuring appropriate prescribing and dispensing; encouraging greater use of generics; and lowering medicine prices.

recommendations.title: Continue to expand access to publicly financed non-emergency dental care
recommendations.text: This can be achieved by going beyond the limited services provided at present – particularly for people with low incomes, who currently experience high levels of unmet need.

recommendations.title: Continue to monitor and address long waiting times and informal payments, ensuring that existing and new measures do not exacerbate inequalities in access to health care
Continue to strengthen the purchasing and governance of publicly financed health care, so that public resources are better able to meet equity and efficiency goals
Support these efforts by increasing the priority given to health in allocating the government budget
recommendations.text: Although public spending on health has risen since the economic crisis, it remains well below the EU average as a share of GDP. In itself, however, an increase in public spending on health is not a guarantee of better financial protection. Any additional public spending on health should be carefully used to reduce financial hardship and unmet need for households with low incomes.

countries.recommendationsSource: Source: [‘Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in Greece' (2025)]( https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/382008).

countries.name: Israel
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2022)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 2.3% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 5.4% of households
* Main drivers: dental care and outpatient medicines on average and especially for low-income households


**Unmet need**

Internationally comparable data on unmet need are not available for Israel, but see the country report on financial protection for national data on unmet need for health care and dental care.

[Israel page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Israel)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Undocumented migrants and most non-working refugees and asylum seekers have very limited access to publicly financed health care: emergency care and some primary care and specialist care for selected conditions only. If they are employed, they are required to be covered by mandatory private health insurance purchased by employers and jointly funded by employers (who must pay at least two thirds of the flat-rate premium cost) and employees. However, insurers offering this form of coverage are not required to cover pre-existing conditions or childbirth and it is difficult to enforce mandatory private health insurance for undocumented migrants. The children (< 18) of undocumented migrants and children (< 18) without a visa can only be covered if their parents pay a health contribution and they lose their coverage if their parents fail to pay it for more than 6 months.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: The National Health Insurance scheme offers only limited coverage of dental care for adults aged between 19 and 72, glasses (only covered for children < 8), psychotherapy and long-term care at home. Waiting times are an issue for publicly financed elective surgical procedures, specialist outpatient care, imaging diagnostic tests, rehabilitation and child development care.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Primary care visits, visits to some specialists (paediatrics, gynaecology and internal medicine) and inpatient care are free at the point of use but user charges are applied to all other outpatient health care and the design of these co-payments is complex. Percentage co-payments are applied to outpatient prescribed medicines and although there is a cap on these co-payments for people with chronic conditions, there are no exemptions for people with low incomes. All households benefit from a separate cap on co-payments for outpatient specialist visits and diagnostic tests, but there is no overall cap on all user charges. Neither of the caps is linked to income and income-based exemptions are usually only available for people > 65.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a complementary role, covering services excluded from or not so well covered by the NHI scheme (e.g. dental care, child development services and occupational therapy), and a supplementary role, providing people with faster access to and greater choice of private treatment (including in public hospitals). Although VHI covers over 80% of the population and accounts for a relatively high share of current spending on health (12% in 2023), it presents several challenges for equity and efficiency: take-up of VHI is much higher in richer than poorer households; VHI premiums represent an additional financial burden on households; VHI does not address gaps caused by user charges; and it plays a very limited role in addressing gaps in dental care coverage. As a result, VHI exacerbates inequalities in access to health care and undermines efficiency by skewing health care resources towards richer households and drawing health care professionals away from publicly financed providers.

recommendations.title: Expand coverage of publicly financed dental care
recommendations.text: Improve National Health Insurance (NHI) coverage of dental care, particularly for children and adults with low incomes.

recommendations.title: Improve co-payment policy
recommendations.text: Reduce co-payments (discounts) for people receiving welfare support from the National Insurance Institute as a first step towards exempting people with low incomes from all co-payments; unify existing co-payment caps by extending them to all co-payments and linking them to income, so that they are more protective for people with lower incomes; and replace percentage co-payments for medicines with low, fixed (flat-rate) co-payments.

recommendations.title: Strengthen population coverage for non-permanent residents
recommendations.text: Improve access to coverage for non-permanent resident children by breaking the link between their entitlement to publicly financed health care and payment of contributions by their parents, and extend coverage for non-permanent resident adults who are not employed.

recommendations.title: Reduce the need for VHI
recommendations.text: The Government should find ways to curb the growth of VHI providing faster access to care and limit dual coverage (holding VHI from a health plan and a commercial insurer). Israel’s experience, echoed by international experience, shows that when this type of VHI is allowed to play a significant role in the health system, it undermines equity and efficiency by exacerbating gaps in access to care based on income and VHI ownership. Part of the solution lies in bringing down waiting times for publicly financed health care to more acceptable levels, finding ways to prevent doctors from shifting users from public to private practice and improving access to health care in peripheral areas.

recommendations.title: Sustain and increase public spending on health
recommendations.text: Public spending on health should rise as a share of the government budget and as a share of GDP so that it is in line with Israel’s level of economic development. Additional funds can be used to reduce financial hardship and unmet need in the ways set out above.

countries.recommendationsSource: Source: 'Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in Israel' (in press).

countries.name: Italy
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2022)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 3.7% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 8.6% of households
* Main drivers: dental care and outpatient medicines on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 2.5% of people
* Dental care: 2.9% of people

[Italy page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Italy)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text:
Entitlement to publicly financed health care is based on residence, which means all 
registered residents (including refugees and asylum seekers) are automatically covered. 
Undocumented adults only have access to publicly financed emergency care, public 
health programmes and maternity care. A recent report indicates that about 500 000 
undocumented migrants live in Italy.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text:
The publicly financed benefits package does not cover most dental care for adults. 
Coverage of dental care for children and medical products is limited.

Procedures and deadlines for updating the benefits package (the Livelli Essenziali di 
Assistenza in Italian, or the LEA) are specified in law but rarely followed, so the benefits 
package is not regularly updated.

Waiting times are a major issue for non-urgent inpatient and outpatient specialist care 
and diagnostic services.

There is significant inequality in access to quality health care between regions in the 
north and the south of the country. Health systems in more deprived regions tend to 
perform less well than those in richer regions.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text:
User charges (co-payments) vary across regions. All regions apply co-payments to 
medical products, outpatient specialist visits, diagnostic tests and dental care. For 
outpatient prescribed medicines, all regions apply reference pricing (“avoidable co-payments”) and 12 out of 21 NHS regions also apply fixed co-payments.

Although there are exemptions in place for several groups of people with low incomes, 
including very young children, pensioners and unemployed people, there are none for 
workers with low incomes or to mitigate “avoidable co-payments” caused by reference 
pricing and there is no overall cap on co-payments.

People can claim an annual tax refund equal to 19% of any out-of-pocket payments 
above €129 but this policy favours people with higher incomes.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a supplementary role (offering faster access to treatment and greater choice of provider) and a complementary role (covering user charges and excluded services) and is provided by non-profit ‘health funds’ and commercial (for-profit) insurers. In 2023 VHI accounted for 2% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Address long waiting times for outpatient specialist visits and diagnostic tests
recommendations.text: Although reducing waiting times is a high priority on the political agenda, further efforts should aim to expand capacity through additional financial resources and enhanced productivity, including reducing inappropriate use of care by establishing clear clinical guidelines for health care providers.

recommendations.title: Improve the design of co-payments, especially for households with low incomes, and reduce regional variation
recommendations.text: Current co-payment exemptions should be extended to all working-aged people with low incomes and to co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines (including the “avoidable co-payments” caused by reference pricing). The Government should also introduce a cap on all co-payments for the whole population – ideally, the cap would be linked to household income so that it is more protective for people with lower incomes and has less impact on the NHS budget.

recommendations.title: Reduce “avoidable co-payments” for more expensive medicines when cheaper alternatives are available
recommendations.text: This can be achieved by encouraging greater use of generics through stronger prescribing and dispensing policies; educational campaigns for users; and extending protection from co-payments (e.g. exemptions) to “avoidable co-payments” caused by reference pricing.

recommendations.title: Review the tax rebate on out-of-pocket payments
recommendations.text: Review the equity and efficiency of the 19% tax rebate on out-of-pocket payments, which tends to favour people with higher incomes.

recommendations.title: Expand NHS coverage of dental care and medical products
recommendations.text: Expand the benefits package for dental care and medical products, including hearing aids and optical care, particularly for people with low incomes.

recommendations.title: Address regional inequalities in access to health care
recommendations.text: Options include improving care quality in the worst-performing regions and covering travel costs for people with low incomes who need highly specialized care in other regions (especially for cancer and rare diseases).

recommendations.title: Close gaps in population coverage
recommendations.text: This can be done by extending entitlement to NHS benefits to adult undocumented migrants, reducing administrative barriers to entitlements and better monitoring. Countries like Spain and France offer examples of good practice in extending coverage to adult undocumented migrants.

recommendations.title: Ensure that levels of public spending on health are adequate to meet population health needs
recommendations.text: To meet equity and efficiency goals now and in the future, particularly in the context of population ageing, the Government should ensure that levels of public spending on health are sufficient and carefully targeted to reduce financial hardship and unmet need for  households with low incomes. It should also find ways to improve equity across regions.

countries.recommendationsSource:
Source: [‘Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in Italy' (2025)]( https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/381967).
See the coverage policy checklist for country examples of good practice in improving financial protection.
