countries.name: Latvia
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2016)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 4.2% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 15% of households
* Most at risk: lower-income households and people with medical cards
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines on average and especially for low-income households

**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 7.6% of people
* Dental care: 9% of people

[Latvia page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Latvia)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Because entitlement to publicly financed health care is based on residence, population coverage is near universal; all permanent residents are automatically covered and refugees are entitled to the same benefits as residents. The main gap in population coverage is for asylum seekers, who are only entitled to a limited set of publicly financed health care (primary care visits and treatment, psychiatric care and emergency care) and undocumented migrants, who are only entitled to publicly financed emergency care.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage of dental care for adults and medical products (glasses and hearing aids) is limited. Other types of health care that are not well covered include physiotherapy and rehabilitation, occupational health care, psychotherapy and termination of pregnancy (without medical justification). Waiting times are an issue for imaging diagnostic tests, some types of outpatient care (physiotherapy and rehabilitation) and some types of surgery[

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to all types of health care, including in the form of percentage co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines and medical products (which are also subject to balance billing), but there are exemptions for people with low incomes, children and on the basis of health-related criteria. Although there is a cap on co-payments, the cap does not apply to co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines or medical products and is not linked to income.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI does not play a significant role in filling gaps in coverage. It plays a mixed complementary (covering some dental care, some diagnostic tests and some co-payments) and supplementary role (providing people with faster access to health care with long waiting times) and is likely mainly to cover people with higher incomes. It does not play any role in filling gaps in population coverage. In 2023 VHI covered around 24% of the population and in 2023 it accounted for 5.2% of current spending on health (WHO, 2026).

countries.name: Lithuania
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2021)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 2.8% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 9.4% of households
* Main drivers: dental care on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 4.3% of people
* Dental care: 2.3% of people

[Lithuania page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Lithuania)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Entitlement depends on payment of contributions; as a result, around 1% of the population is not covered by the National Health Insurance Fund. Non-covered people are of working age and likely to be working in the informal economy, homeless or working abroad without formally declaring their absence. Around 70% of them are men. Entitlements for refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented migrants are limited to emergency care, maternity care and other urgent essential services.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text:
Coverage of dental care for adults is limited to people receiving income support; everyone else must pay for materials in public dental care centres. The list of covered medicines is relatively limited and does not include over-the-counter medicines

Waiting times are an issue for family doctor visits, specialist consultations and diagnostic tests. Although there are waiting time guarantees in place, these have not been sufficiently effective.

Informal payments in outpatient and inpatient care are also an issue.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges in the form of reference pricing are applied to outpatient prescribed medicines and people with low incomes are only exempt if they are retired or have a disability, but there is a cap on how much people have to pay through reference pricing if they choose the cheapest option. Reference pricing also applies to diagnostic tests, without any protection mechanism.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a minor supplementary role, mainly offering access to private health care providers. A 2018 survey indicates that around 12% of employees have VHI. In 2022 it accounted for 1.6% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

countries.name: Luxembourg
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2020)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 2.5% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 3.9% of households
* Most at risk: lower-income households and older people
* Main drivers: medical products on average and especially for low-income households

**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 1% of people
* Dental care: 1.3% of people

[Luxembourg page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Luxembourg)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text:
The main basis for entitlement is payment of contributions to the National Health Fund, which creates a gap in coverage for those who are unable to pay. People in vulnerable situations who cannot pay contributions and are not eligible for social welfare support can obtain coverage by applying to the universal health care coverage pilot set up in 2022, but the number of beneficiaries has been low in relation to the number of people likely to be in need (only 300 as of February 2025).

Refugees are entitled to the same publicly financed benefits as other residents. Asylum seekers are entitled to limited publicly financed health care during a probationary period of three months, after which they are entitled to the same publicly financed benefits as residents.

Undocumented migrant adults are not entitled to any type of publicly financed health care. The children of undocumented migrants are not automatically covered[ST4.1]. 

Around 7% of the resident population was not covered by the National Health Fund in 2023. Non-covered people include those who do not pay contributions (undocumented migrants), those who do not benefit from the universal health care coverage pilot set up in 2022, EU civil servants (who are covered by a separate EU scheme) and workers who have been in Luxembourg for less than a year and are covered by a health insurance scheme in another country.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: There are volume limits on doctor consultations and on psychotherapy and physiotherapy sessions. Coverage of optical products (glasses or contact lenses) and some types of dental care is also limited. Retrospective reimbursement applies to some outpatient visits (consultations), which means that people have to pay out of pocket first and then apply for reimbursement from the National Health Fund if their doctor or dentist does not use the ‘direct Immediate payment’ system. This may be a barrier to access for households with low incomes.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: There are user charges for all types of care, mainly in the form of percentage co-payments. Balance billing is applied to outpatient primary care visits, outpatient specialist visits, inpatient care and dental care. Dental care treatment is also subject to extra billing. Although there is a cap on most co-payments, and the cap is linked to income, it is not applied automatically and it does not cover balance or extra billing.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI accounted for 3.3% of current spending on health in 2024 and covered 67.3% of the population in 2022 (the latest available year of data). VHI does not play a role in filling gaps in population coverage. It covers gaps in service coverage to a limited extent, as it plays a supplementary role covering services already included in the publicly financed benefits package and offering access to enhanced benefits or amenities. VHI covers co-payments for some types of care (inpatient care, dental care and optical care). Coverage varies according to the insurer and insurance plan.

countries.name: Malta
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2015)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 2.2% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 6.9% of households
* Main drivers: dental care and outpatient medicines on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 0.3% of people
* Dental care: 0.2% of people

[Malta page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Malta)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Undocumented migrants with no protection status, asylum seekers whose application for asylum has been refused and people granted humanitarian protection by another European Union member state have no entitlement to publicly financed health care beyond life-saving medical assistance. Asylum seekers and applicants for international protection are only entitled to emergency care, essential treatment and treatment of serious mental disorders.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: The publicly financed benefits package does not cover non-emergency dental care or optical care and only covers outpatient prescribed medicines, dentures and some medical products (glasses and prosthetic aids) for about 30% of the population (mainly people with selected chronic conditions and people with low incomes); the rest of the population must pay the full price out of pocket for all outpatient prescribed medicines, dentures and medical products. Waiting times are an issue, although there are policies in place to address them. People tend to access outpatient primary care in private settings due to shorter waiting times and better continuity of care. Due to a lack of resources or the small number of people affected, some health care cannot be provided in Malta and requires treatment abroad.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Although there are no user charges for covered health care, most people have to pay the full price out of pocket for all outpatient prescribed medicines, non-emergency dental care, medical products and optical care.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a mixed supplementary and complementary (services) role. VHI plays a supplementary role, providing faster access to treatment and greater choice of health care provider. It also plays a complementary (services) role, mainly covering dental care, optical care, chiropractor, osteopathy and prosthetics. In 2021 VHI accounted for 2.9% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Find ways to improve protection from out-of-pocket payments for households with low incomes – for example, by leveraging existing means-testing mechanisms
recommendations.text: The pink card scheme only covers 3% of the population and is also limited in terms of the medicines and medical products it covers.

recommendations.title: Use digital solutions to monitor the types of outpatient prescribed medicines households are spending on to inform policy options for reducing out-of-pocket payments and improving financial certainty for all households
recommendations.text: Many countries with stronger financial protection have some kind of cap on out-of-pocket payments for covered health care: linking a cap to income (and using digital tools to ensure it is applied automatically) enhances equity and efficiency in the use of public funds and softens the impact of the cap on the health budget.

recommendations.title: Reduce out-of-pocket payments for non-emergency dental care
recommendations.text: This can be done by extending publicly financed coverage of non-emergency dental care to those most likely to benefit in the short term, such as pregnant women and people with pink cards; and expanding the range of publicly financed non-emergency dental care, going beyond the services currently provided.

recommendations.title: Continue efforts to lower the price of outpatient medicines and address long waiting times for publicly financed outpatient care
Increase public spending on health so that it is more in line with Malta’s GDP
recommendations.text: There is scope for increasing the share of public spending on health given Malta’s sustained and current GDP growth. The Government should focus public resources on reducing financial hardship and unmet need, particularly for households with low incomes.

recommendations.title: Strengthen the commissioning (the purchasing and governance) of publicly financed health care, so that public resources are better able to meet equity and efficiency goals

Source: [‘Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in Malta' (2025)](https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/381464).

countries.name: North Macedonia
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2024)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 5.3% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 9.3% of households
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines on average and especially for low-income households


**Unmet need (2023)**

* Health care: 2.7% of people
* Dental care: 3.3% of people

[North Macedonia page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/NorthMacedonia)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Given that the basis for entitlement is linked to payment of contributions, people without regular employment, self-employed people who have not paid contributions and people whose employers delay paying wages for more than two months due to liquidity problems are at risk of not being covered. Undocumented migrants and others who are not covered are only entitled to publicly financed emergency care.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: The positive list for outpatient prescribed medicines is narrow in scope and not updated regularly. Public hospitals are characterised by poor service quality and infrastructure. Informal payments are common in gynaecology in primary care.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to most health services and are in the form of percentage co-payments ranging from 0% to 20% of the reference price. People with low incomes are not exempt from co-payments for outpatient medicines and medical products.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: Supplementary VHI offers people access to non-contracted private facilities and use of private rooms and access to services outside working hours in public facilities. Complementary VHI covers co-payments for publicly financed health care but take-up is extremely low. The number of VHI contracts was around 1.8% of the population in 2023 but contracts typically cover dependants so the actual share of the population covered by VHI is slightly higher than 1.8% (ISA, 2024). In 2022 VHI accounted for 2.6% of current spending on health (WHO, 2025). Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Further expand the coverage and accessibility of cost-effective outpatient medicines
recommendations.text: Building on the recent expansion of the positive list of outpatient medicines, the Health Insurance Fund (HIF) should give priority to further expanding the list; align the list with national clinical guidelines; relax prescribing rules so that common chronic conditions can be treated by family doctors; and ensure that cost-effective medicines and diagnostic tests are available in primary care, starting with those listed in national clinical guidelines.

recommendations.title: Improve efficiency and equity in the use of medicines
recommendations.text: The HIF and the Ministry of Health should continue to work with health care providers and pharmacies to ensure appropriate prescribing and dispensing and encourage greater use of generic medicines. Options include systematically monitoring prescribing and dispensing, starting with the universal enforcement of electronic prescribing; making generic substitution in pharmacies mandatory, so that people always benefit from the lowest-priced alternative; strengthening regulation to limit the influence of pharmaceutical companies on prescribing and dispensing behaviour; and monitoring the prevalence of different types of co-payments and protection from co-payments using existing digital tools.

recommendations.title: Strengthen co-payment design to protect people with low incomes from all co-payments
recommendations.text: This could be done by exempting the cost-effective outpatient medicines and diagnostic tests included in the national clinical guidelines from co-payments; exempting households with low incomes from all co-payments; extending the annual cap on co-payments to all co-payments; and where feasible, replacing percentage co-payments with low, fixed co-payments.

recommendations.title: Reduce the “avoidable co-payments” caused by reference pricing, which account for around 40% of co-payments for outpatient medicines
recommendations.text: This could be done by ensuring that at least one medicine in each reference group is available at the reference price; waiving reference pricing when higher-priced alternatives are prescribed for therapeutic reasons; aligning reference prices and maximum retail prices; and monitoring the availability of medicines at the reference price in pharmacies.

recommendations.title: Abolish balance billing
recommendations.text: Balance billing reduces transparency and financial certainty for people accessing health care. Very few countries in Europe use balance billing and those that do are trying to eliminate it.

recommendations.title: Monitor and reduce waiting times and informal payments and control the use of private care in public and private facilities
recommendations.text: Collecting administrative data and, where necessary, survey data, would help to assess the magnitude of waiting times, informal payments and the use of and interaction between private care in public and private facilities; increase understanding of their effect on households and the health system; and identify strategies to curb any negative impact on efficiency and equity in the use of limited financial and human resources for health.

recommendations.title: Improve the collection of health spending data in the household budget survey by aligning methods with international standards
recommendations.text: This could be done by extending the recall period for less frequent but high-cost types of care (e.g. inpatient care) and improving the disaggregation level of data on household spending on health to allow better estimation of the main drivers of financial hardship.

recommendations.title: Ensure universal and permanent population coverage for adults and children
recommendations.text: Options include (i) ensuring that people (and their dependants) do not lose HIF coverage when they experience a change in their work circumstances or employers fail to pay wages on time; and (ii) changing the basis for entitlement to HIF benefits from payment of mandatory health insurance contributions to residence (as in other countries in Europe with social health insurance schemes). This change would ensure that all residents are entitled to the same health care benefits, throughout the life course, and that non-payment of mandatory contributions are treated in the same way as non-payment of other taxes (e.g. using fines, when relevant, rather than denying people access to health care).

recommendations.title: Broaden the public revenue base for the health system to reduce reliance on employment-based contributions (payroll taxes), so that public revenue for health does not shrink as the population ages
recommendations.text: Options include (i) making greater use of government budget transfers to the HIF; and (ii) extending the levy base for some or all of the mandatory health insurance contribution to non-wage forms of income.

recommendations.title: Support these efforts by increasing the priority given to health in allocating the government budget and ensuring that any additional public investment is carefully used to meet equity and efficiency goals

countries.recommendationsSource:
Source: [‘Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in North Macedonia' (2025)]( https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/384538).

countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2022)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 0.7% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 2.8% of households
* Main drivers: medical products and dental care on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households

**Unmet need (2024)**

[Norway page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Norway)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Because the basis for entitlement is permanent residence, most of the population is covered. However, people without a residence or working permit (including undocumented migrants and asylum seekers who are not registered with a reception centre) are entitled to publicly financed emergency care, childbirth and treatment of communicable diseases only. Administrative barriers may delay access to health care for asylum seekers due to the time it takes to process applications for asylum and residence.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Dental care coverage is limited and only available to children < 28. Glasses and contact lenses are not typically covered for adults. Long waiting times are an issue for specialist care.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to all health care except inpatient care and generally apply to anyone > 16. The only low-income households exempt from some co-payments (for outpatient prescribed medicines, medical products and diagnostic tests) are pensioners who receive a minimum old-age or disability pension. Although there is an annual cap on co-payments but it does not cover balance billing or extra billing for non-covered clinical services.

countries.name: Poland
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2021)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 3.3% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 9.4% of households
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines on average and especially for low-income households


**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 3.8% of people
* Dental care: 1.3% of people

[Poland page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Poland)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Because entitlement is based on enrolment in the National Health Fund (NHF) and payment of mandatory contributions, the following groups of people may lack NHF coverage: people working in the informal sector, unemployed people who have not registered with the unemployment office and homeless people who have not registered with social assistance institutions. Some groups of people are not subject to mandatory NHF coverage (e.g. volunteers, people with short-term contracts for specific tasks, employees on unpaid leave) and may also lack coverage. Undocumented migrants are only entitled to emergency care provided in non-hospital settings in life-threatening situations.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Waiting times for specialist care. A shortage of medical professionals. Limited coverage of dental care, particularly for adults and a limited supply of publicly financed dental care, particularly in rural areas. Volume and frequency limits on entitlement to medical products and rehabilitation. Informal payments and paying physicians in private practice to obtain better or faster treatment in the publicly financed part of the system are also issues.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Percentage co-payments and reference pricing are applied to outpatient prescribed medicines and some medical products. Although children are exempt from co-payments and people > 65 are exempt from co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines, there are no exemptions from any co-payments for people with low incomes and there is no cap on co-payments.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a mainly supplementary role covering primary care and outpatient specialist care and, less commonly, hospital care or highly specialised diagnostics. In 2023 around 13% of the population (4.7 million) had VHI. These statistics do not include people with so-called medical subscription packages. In 2022 it accounted for 5.4% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

countries.name: Portugal
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2022)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 3.3% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 7.5% of households
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines on average and especially for low-income households


**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 2.5% of people
* Dental care: 7.9% of people

[Portugal page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Portugal)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Entitlement is based on residence, so there are no gaps in population coverage for permanent residents. Refugees, asylum seekers, the children of undocumented migrants and some undocumented migrant adults are entitled to the same benefits as residents; however, administrative barriers may hinder access to health care for these groups of people.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text:
Access to dental care is restricted due to the lack of sufficient public facilities. Corrective lenses are limited to people over 65 years with low incomes receiving social support only.

Waiting times are an issue, particularly for outpatient specialist visits and elective surgery and partly due to a shortage of health professionals. Waiting time targets are often exceeded. As a result, people with high incomes resort to treatment in the private sector.

The archipelagos experience access challenges, especially in the Azores; not all islands have hospitals and transport can be affected by weather conditions.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to most types of care except primary care visits, diagnostic tests in primary care and inpatient care. Percentage co-payments of up to 85% are applied to outpatient prescribed medicines and medical products. Very few people with low incomes (older people receiving social support only) are exempt from co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines, there are no exemptions from co-payments for medical products and existing exemptions are not applied automatically. There is no cap on co-payments. People may pay more than expected out-of-pocket for covered medicines as the lowest-priced alternatives are not always available in pharmacies.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a supplementary role providing people with faster access to health care or increased choice of provider and is provided by two types of entities: so called subsystems and commercial insurance companies. In 2023 31% of the population had some form of VHI and subsystem and commercial VHI together accounted for 7.6% of current spending on health in 2023. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Enhance access to outpatient prescribed medicines as part of primary care
recommendations.text: Options include replacing percentage co-payments with low fixed co-payments (which are more transparent); ensuring people can access at least one of the three lowest-priced medicines in each reference group free at the point of use; monitoring prescribing patterns, including the role of generic medicines; making generic substitution mandatory in pharmacies (but allowing users to opt for a more expensive alternative if they prefer); introducing penalties for pharmacies that are not able to provide people immediately with the lowest-priced medicine; and avoiding further increases in medicine prices.

recommendations.title: Improve mechanisms to protect people with low incomes from co-payments, especially co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines
recommendations.text: Extend exemptions from outpatient prescribed medicines to all people with low incomes, not just pensioners; introduce a cap on all co-payments and link the cap to household income; and make sure exemptions and caps are applied automatically, using digital tools, for everyone.

recommendations.title: Continue with efforts to reduce waiting times and improve access to primary care
recommendations.text: Closely monitor waiting times to make sure targets are met. Facilitate access to NHS family doctors by ensuring sufficient staff numbers and enhancing the role of other health professionals in providing care (e.g. nurses, dentists, psychologists and social workers) to increase access to primary care.

recommendations.title: Expand access to publicly financed dental care
recommendations.text: Options include extending the number of municipalities in the pilot project on access to dental care in NHS primary care centres; implementing planned investment in dedicated offices for dental care in primary care; selectively contracting private providers where needed; and simplifying the dental care voucher system – for example, by extending vouchers to all people with low incomes, without time or volume limits on care.

recommendations.title: Expand coverage of medical products, especially for people with low incomes
recommendations.text: Add corrective lenses (e.g. glasses) to the benefits package and reduce heavy user charges for covered medical products (currently percentage co-payments ranging from 15% to 85% of the price), particularly for people with low incomes.

recommendations.title: Evaluate the benefits and costs of tax subsidies for out-of-pocket payments and VHI premiums
recommendations.text: These tax subsidies typically favour richer households and shift public resources away from health need. Public resources are more likely to meet equity and efficiency goals if they are used to reduce financial hardship and unmet need for households with low incomes.

[Republic of Moldova page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Moldova)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: In 2022 about 13.5% of the population entitled to coverage was not covered by the National Health Insurance Company (CNAM). Those most likely to lack CNAM coverage are working-age people, unemployed people, inactive or self-employed people, people working in agriculture and living in poorer households and in rural areas and migrants without temporary or permanent resident permits. All residents, regardless of coverage status, and Ukrainian refugees with temporary protection status, are entitled to emergency care, outpatient primary care visits, treatment of selected diseases and outpatient medicines and medical products for selected conditions, without user charges. Refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented migrants can only access emergency care.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage of outpatient prescribed medicines, diagnostic tests and medical products is limited. Coverage of non-emergency dental care is also limited. Waiting times are an issue, particularly for diagnostic services and for some types of outpatient specialist visit in public hospitals. Informal payments are widespread, mainly in inpatient settings.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are applied to outpatient medicines and medical products, usually in the form of reference pricing. Other covered health care is free at the point of use with referral but people tend to pay the full price out of pocket for inpatient supplies (informal payments), for non-covered services and for covered outpatient care without a referral to avoid waiting lists.

gaps.text: Around 13% of people entitled to publicly financed coverage are not covered by the National Health Insurance House (NHIH), including people entitled but not registered for unemployment or social benefits and people living or working abroad but still domiciled in Romania.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage of dental care is limited. Access to health care may be hindered by shortages of human resources, medical supplies (e.g. medicines and diagnostic tests) and health facilities, especially in rural areas. Informal payments to health workers are widespread and high, particularly in public hospitals.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Co-payments are applied to outpatient medicines, medical products, dental treatment and inpatient care, often in the form of percentage co-payments. There is no general protection from user charges for people with low incomes and there is no overall cap on co-payments. Extra billing (for superior accommodation in public hospitals) and balance billing (for publicly financed inpatient care in private facilities) are permitted.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a very minor supplementary role, offering people access to superior accommodation in hospitals, free choice of provider and access to treatment in private facilities. It accounted for 0.5% of current spending on health in 2020 and covered around 2% of the population in 2021. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Break the link between access to health care and health insurance status
recommendations.text: Ensure that the whole population is covered by the National Health Insurance House (NHIH) and has access to the same set of benefits. The Government can begin to pay NHIH contributions for people living below the poverty line who are not entitled to social support. It should also consider de-linking entitlement from payment of NHIH contributions; addressing non-payment of contributions should be the responsibility of the tax agency (not the health system).

recommendations.title: Improve protection from co-payments and other out-of-pocket payments for households with low incomes
recommendations.text: Extend exemptions from co-payments to households with low incomes and introduce an income-based cap on all co-payments. Limit balance billing and extra billing. Monitor and address the root causes of informal payments and improve service quality in public inpatient facilities.

recommendations.title: Strengthen the coverage and purchasing of medicines and dental services
recommendations.text: Continue to improve the way in which the NHIH purchases medicines, including over-the-counter medicines. Strengthen the coverage and purchasing of dental care to address high levels of unmet need in the poorest households and financial hardship for other households.

recommendations.title: Increase public spending on health and use resources to meet equity and efficiency goals
recommendations.text: Increase public spending on health and ensure that any additional funds are carefully allocated to reduce inequalities in access to health care.

countries.name: Serbia
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2022)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 9.4% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 14.4% of households
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines on average and especially for low-income households


**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 6.8% of people
* Dental care: 5.6% of people

[Serbia page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Serbia)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: The basis for entitlement is payment of contributions. As a result, about 3% of the population were not covered in 2020. People who have not paid contributions, people whose employers delay paying contributions, undocumented migrants and others who do not hold a health insurance card are only entitled to publicly financed emergency care, maternity care and child care. People need to show a valid health insurance card to receive publicly financed non-emergency health care, which may present an administrative barrier to access for some people.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage of dental care and medical products (e.g. glasses and hearing aids) is limited. Waiting times are an issue, particularly for diagnostics and surgery, and waiting time guarantees are often exceeded. Informal payments to health care workers are also an issue due to weak enforcement of anti-corruption laws. Some people may face administrative barriers to obtaining a health insurance card, which is needed to access publicly financed health care.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Co-payments are applied to all types of health care except emergency care, mainly in the form of percentage co-payments (including for inpatient care). However, there are exemptions from co-payments based on income, age and other factors, and an annual income-based cap on co-payments for outpatient and inpatient care, including outpatient prescribed medicines.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: Country information coming soon

recommendations.title: Reduce out-of-pocket payments for outpatient prescribed medicines
recommendations.text: This could be done by broadening the list of medicines and clinical indications covered; replacing percentage co-payments with low, fixed co-payments; taking steps to ensure rational prescribing and dispensing; and improving the monitoring of spending on medicines. Further analysis can help to identify the steps needed to improve the coverage, availability, prescribing and dispensing of outpatient medicines.

recommendations.title: Strengthen existing protection from co-payments
recommendations.text: This could be done by exempting more households with low incomes; lowering the annual cap on co-payments, particularly for people with low incomes; automating the cap for everyone; removing financial penalties for people not attending preventive programmes; and monitoring the effectiveness of these mechanisms.

recommendations.title: Continue to address long waiting lists and make information about waiting times publicly available
recommendations.text: Enhancing transparency would improve the accountability of the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) and health care providers.

recommendations.title: Improve the coverage of medical products
recommendations.text: This could be done by updating the list of covered products and replacing percentage co-payments with low, fixed co-payments.

recommendations.title: Improve dental care coverage
recommendations.text: Extend service coverage to working-aged adults with low incomes and replace percentage co-payments with low, fixed co-payments.

recommendations.title: Systematically monitor population coverage and extend NHIF coverage to the whole population
recommendations.text: First, ensure that employed people whose employers have not paid mandatory contributions on their behalf do not lose coverage; second, instead of penalizing people who do not pay mandatory contributions by removing their access to health care, leave it to the tax agency to enforce payment in the same way it enforces non-payment of other taxes (e.g. using fines, when relevant); and third, ensure that access to care is not denied to people who are covered but unable to present a valid health insurance card.

recommendations.title: Strengthen the governance of the health system and the capacity of the NHIF to act as a strategic purchaser by improving the availability and use of data by the Ministry of Health and the NHIF
recommendations.text: Better data collection, monitoring and reporting systems will help to identify areas where efficiency and equity can be improved.

countries.name: Slovakia
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2023)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 3.3% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 4.4% of households
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines and dental care on average; outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need (2024)**

* Health care: 1.6% of people
* Dental care: 1.4% of people

[Slovakia page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Slovakia)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text:
The basis for entitlement to SHI benefits is payment of mandatory contributions by people or by the Government on behalf of selected groups. In 2022 around 5% of the eligible population (246 058 people) was not covered by the SHI scheme – mainly people working in other EU countries and homeless people.

People who fail to pay their contributions for three months, homeless people, asylum seekers who are unemployed and other people not eligible for SHI or not covered by the SHI scheme have access only to publicly financed emergency care, maternity care and treatment of communicable diseases.

Undocumented migrants are not entitled to any publicly financed health care.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage of dental care and glasses is limited. Waiting times are an issue for outpatient care. Informal payments are also widespread in outpatient care, mainly because health care providers charge people for services such as a first visit to a clinic, setting up a patient file or ambulance running costs. Roma people living in segregated settlements in eastern Slovakia experience additional access barriers.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text:
User charges are applied to emergency care, outpatient prescribed medicines, medical products and dental care treatment, usually in the form of fixed co-payments. There are protection mechanisms in place, but these are quite narrow: reduced co-payments only apply to emergency care, while exemptions and caps on co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines and medical products only apply to children under 6 years old, pensioners with low incomes and people who have a disability with low incomes.

Extra billing for non-clinical services occurs in outpatient and inpatient care settings.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays an extremely small supplementary role, covering care in case of accident or illness, medical costs incurred abroad or the cost of mountain rescue in emergency cases. In 2015 0.6% of the population had VHI. No information is available on the VHI share of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Ensure people have access to outpatient prescribed medicines without co-payments
recommendations.text: This can be achieved by including at least one medicine with a €0 co-payment medicine in every reference group; guaranteeing the availability of this medicine in pharmacies throughout the country; strengthening adherence to clinical guidelines and INN prescribing by doctors, as well as generic substitution in pharmacies; and simplifying the system of co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines to a single co-payment for all medicines incurring co-payments over €1 – this would also enhance transparency, equity and efficiency.

recommendations.title: Improve the mechanisms used to protect people from co-payments by extending exemptions and caps to all co-payments, to all people with low incomes and, ideally, to people with chronic conditions
recommendations.text: These mechanisms should be applied automatically, to ensure everyone eligible benefits from them, and accompanied by regular monitoring to ensure their scope is appropriate.

recommendations.title: Reassess the usefulness of co-payments for emergency care by tackling the root causes of overuse of emergency care
recommendations.text: Although co-payments for emergency care are in the form of relatively low and transparent fixed co-payments, and some people are exempt in certain circumstances, they are unlikely to address the real reasons why people use emergency services – that is, because of a lack of sufficient access to primary care (including treatment in primary care settings).

recommendations.title: Expand publicly financed coverage of dental care
recommendations.text: This can be done by covering the use of higher-quality materials and finding ways to ensure that more providers offer covered services.

recommendations.title: Tackle inefficiencies in the health system that push people to pay out of pocket for covered care
recommendations.text:
This can be done by systematically monitoring and enforcing waiting time targets (e.g. those introduced for elective surgery from 2025); closely monitoring the causes and effects of informal payments by establishing regular surveillance and reporting mechanisms; and closing loopholes in the law that enable providers to extra bill people in outpatient and inpatient care settings.

Soften the link between entitlement to SHI benefits and payment of mandatory SHI contributions. This means stopping penalizing people who are unable to pay contributions by denying them access to health care.

Expand the scope of publicly financed health care that is available to people who are not eligible to be covered by the SHI scheme.

Broaden the public revenue base so that is it able to generate sufficient funding as the population ages.

recommendations.title: Soften the link between entitlement to SHI benefits and payment of mandatory SHI contributions
recommendations.text: This can be achieved by stopping penalizing people who are not able to pay contributions by denying them access to health care, as in Czechia where people continue to have full access to HIIS benefits, even if they have not paid mandatory contributions.

recommendations.title: Expand the scope of publicly financed health care that is available to people who are not eligible for or not covered by the SHI scheme
Broaden the public revenue base so that is it able to generate sufficient funding as the population ages and meet equity and efficiency goals, now and in the future

countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2022)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 0.2% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 1.6% of households
* Main drivers: dental care on average; medical products, dental care, outpatient care and outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 3.2% of people
* Dental care: 3.9% of people

[Slovenia page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Slovenia)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text:
Entitlement to the Health Insurance Institute of Slovenia (HIIS) benefits is based on legal residence and payment of mandatory contributions to the HIIS. Undocumented migrants are 
not eligible for HIIS coverage. At the end of 2024 about 0.6% of the eligible population was not fully entitled to HIIS benefits; 0.5% due to non-payment of contributions (mainly self-employed people) and 0.1% due to administrative barriers (e.g. people waiting to be recognized as pensioners or unemployed).


Although everyone in Slovenia, regardless of residence status or payment of contributions, is entitled to publicly financed emergency care and a few other services (e.g. selected outpatient medicines, 
selected dental care, pregnancy and childbirth care, contraception and termination of pregnancy) they must pay for all other care out of pocket. People who are eligible for HIIS coverage but have not paid the required contributions can request retrospective reimbursement of out-of-pocket payments incurred for HIIS benefits care once they have settled their debt to the HIIS.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text:
Although the HIIS benefits package is generally comprehensive, there are limitations in the coverage of dental care for adults (which is gradually being expanded) and medical products for visual impairment. Access to covered medical products (corrective lenses and hearing 
aids) may be hindered by limited public awareness of entitlements and misleading advertising by providers.


Waiting times are an issue for outpatient specialist services (including dental care), inpatient care (mainly elective surgery) and some diagnostic tests. They are the main reason for self-reported unmet need for health and dental care and have grown over time.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text:
Reference pricing is applied to outpatient prescribed medicines and medical products and there are no mechanisms to protect people from these “avoidable co-payments”.


Providers can charge covered people extra for non-standard dental treatment for selected procedures (e.g. prostheses and fillings). A few treatments and groups of people are exempt from some of these charges.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI does not generally fill gaps in population coverage. VHI offers faster access to health care for diagnostic tests and other specialist care with long waiting times and can cover extra charges in dental care, but but take up is concentrated in people with higher incomes.

recommendations.title: Broaden the public revenue base for the health system to reduce reliance on employment, so that public revenue for health does not shrink as the population ages
recommendations.text: Options include greater use of government budget transfers to the Social Health Insurance (SHI) scheme and extending the levy base for some or all of the SHI contribution to non-wage forms of income.

recommendations.title: Continue to address long waiting times
recommendations.text: The Government should find ways to bring down waiting times to more acceptable levels and ensure that voluntary health insurance (VHI) offering faster access to treatment does not exacerbate inequalities in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Protect people with low incomes from any remaining user charges for covered health care
recommendations.text: This can be done by exempting people with low incomes from co-payments arising from reference pricing for outpatient prescribed medicines and from extra charges for dental treatment; introducing a cap on all co-payments, ideally linked to income to soften the impact of the cap on the health budget; and applying these protection mechanisms automatically, using digital tools, to ensure all eligible people benefit.

recommendations.title: Avoid introducing or increasing user charges in the future
recommendations.text: A major reform introduced in 2024 abolished most co-payments – an example of good practice to other countries in Europe and beyond. A large body of evidence shows that user charges are not an effective way of directing people to use health care more efficiently and have negative effects on affordable access to health care and other aspects of health system performance.

recommendations.title: Improve the affordability of outpatient medicines, as well as dental care for adults, corrective lenses and hearing aids
recommendations.text: Around 13% of all outpatients prescribed medicines dispensed incur “avoidable co- payments” arising from reference pricing. This share could be reduced by ensuring that health care workers have incentives to prescribe and dispense the cheapest alternatives. It may also be useful to explore why households are spending on over-the-counter (OTC) medicines. Ensure affordable access to adult dental care, corrective lenses and hearing aids by granting standard-quality benefits and promoting proper awareness of entitlements among the public and providers.

recommendations.title: Address the regressivity of the new flat-rate contribution, so that it no longer imposes a much heavier financial burden on people with lower incomes
recommendations.text: The 2024 reform replaced premiums for VHI covering SHI co-payments with a new mandatory flat-rate contribution per person (the Obvezni zdravstveni prispevek, OZP, in Slovenian). Although some groups of people are exempt from the OZP, it is a regressive payment, placing a much heavier financial burden on households with lower incomes.

recommendations.title: Find ways to ensure the whole population is covered
recommendations.text: Options include changing the basis for entitlement to residence (as France did in 2000) or continuing to give people full access to SHI benefits, even if they have not paid mandatory contributions (as in Czechia). This is particularly important after the 2024 reform, as now entitlement to publicly financed health care depends not just on payment of regular SHI contributions but also on payment of the new mandatory flat-rate contribution (the OZP).

countries.name: Spain
countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2020)**

* Impoverishing health spending: 1.6% of households
* Catastrophic health spending: 2.9% of households
* Main drivers: medical products on average; medical products and outpatient medicines for low-income households


**Unmet need (2025)**

* Health care: 1.6% of people
* Dental care: 4.1% of people

[Spain page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Spain)

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: None for residents, but administrative barriers can hinder access to entitlements for undocumented migrants, asylum seekers and foreigners legally reunited with relatives in Spain.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage of dental care, hearing aids and optical care (glasses and contact lenses)is limited, especially for adults. Waiting times are an issue for elective surgery, outpatient specialist visits, diagnostic tests and mental health care.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text:
Percentage co-payments are applied to outpatient prescribed medicines and medical products (ortho-prosthetic devices such as supportive braces and splints, prostheses, wheelchairs, crutches and hearing aids). There are several protection mechanisms in place: a cap per prescription item for many medicines for chronic conditions, a monthly cap on co-payments for prescribed medicines for pensioners and exemptions from co-payments for prescribed medicines and medical products for several groups of disadvantaged people, including some people with low incomes. However, there are no exemptions from co-payments for children and many low-income households, and caps do not apply to non-pensioners.

Access to these protection mechanisms may be hindered by administrative barriers when there is an application process in place (as there is for beneficiaries of the minimum vital income scheme) or delayed until the beginning of the following year because the user database that collects data on income and working status is only updated once a year.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI covers some non-covered services, such as dental care, but mainly plays a supplementary role, providing faster access to access to outpatient specialist care, inpatient care and diagnostic tests. Complementary VHI covered around 11% of the population in 2020 and supplementary VHI covered 21% of the population in 2021. The share of the population with VHI varies widely across regions. In 2020 VHI accounted for 7% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Expand coverage of dental care, hearing aids and optical care
recommendations.text: Address the most important gaps in coverage by expanding publicly financed entitlement to dental care, hearing aids and optical care.

recommendations.title: Reduce co-payments for households with low incomes
recommendations.text: Further improve the design of co-payments to strengthen protection for households with low incomes in all age groups – for example, by extending the income-related cap on co-payments for prescribed medicines to all households.

recommendations.title: Address waiting times for outpatient specialist care
recommendations.text: Policy options to address waiting times include reinforcing the effectiveness of primary care by ensuring it is resourced and staffed adequately; reviewing the efficiency and equity of tax subsidies for voluntary health insurance premiums, which mainly benefit richer households; and reviewing current policy towards mutual funds, which allow civil servants to opt for private provision.

recommendations.title: Remove administrative barriers for undocumented migrants
recommendations.text: Remove the administrative barriers undocumented migrants and others face in obtaining access to services to which they are entitled.

recommendations.title: Increase public spending on health and use resources to meet equity and efficiency goals
recommendations.text: Strengthening financial protection is likely to require additional public spending on health. To ensure additional spending meets equity and efficiency goals, it should be targeted carefully to reduce financial hardship and unmet need for households with low incomes.

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Entitlement to publicly financed health care is based on residence, which means all residents are automatically covered. Adults without a resident permit (e.g. asylum seekers and undocumented migrants), refugees and people under the EU Temporary Protection Directive 2001/55/EC are not entitled to the full range of publicly financed health care and can only access emergency care, with co-payments. Administrative barriers may delay access to health care for migrants due to the lengthy residence permit application process.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: The publicly financed benefits package is relatively comprehensive. However, waiting times are an issue for primary care and outpatient specialist care. They are the main reason for self-reported unmet need for health care, although levels of unmet need for health care are below the European Union average.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Co-payments are applied to most publicly financed health care except diagnostic tests and inpatient medicines. For covered outpatient prescribed medicines, medical products and dental care, patients pay the full price up to a specific threshold. Balance billing is permitted for dental care. No groups of people are exempt from co-payments on the basis of income. Although people with low incomes can apply for retrospective reimbursement of all co-payments, the application process may be an administrative barrier. There is no overall cap on co-payments.

countries.summary:
**Financial hardship (2022)** 

* Impoverishing health spending: 14.5% of households 
* Catastrophic health spending: 17.7% of households 
* Most at-risk: lower-income households, older people and unemployed people 
* Main drivers: outpatient medicines on average and especially for lower-income households 

**Unmet need** 

Internationally comparable data on unmet need are not available for Tajikistan

[Tajikistan page](https://apps.who.int/dhis2/uhcwatch/Tajikistan)

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI plays a very small supplementary role (providing faster access to treatment) and complementary role (covering services not included in the publicly financed benefits package). It does not address gaps in coverage. In 2023 it accounted for less than 0.01% of current spending on health [(WHO, 2026)].

recommendations.title: Expand the benefits package (Decree 600) to include more comprehensive coverage of primary care, including diagnostic tests and outpatient medicines for priority conditions.
recommendations.text: A wider range of cost-effective diagnostic tests and outpatient medicines should be covered with no co-payments (or minimal fixed co-payments) for the whole population. The benefits package should be regularly reviewed and adjusted to reflect population health needs, cost-effectiveness and other explicit criteria; it should also be aligned with the available budget.

recommendations.title: Introduce a new benefits package for outpatient medicines with an explicit list of priority medicines.
recommendations.text: The new benefits package could start by covering a limited number of medicines for common chronic and priority conditions and ensuring that these are available and free at the point of use for users and well-funded at primary care facilities. Prices should be regulated and the list should be expanded over time.

recommendations.title: Strengthen the design of existing co-payments to strengthen protection for people with low incomes.
recommendations.text: This can be achieved by revising the list of groups exempt from co-payments to include those at highest risk of financial hardship and unmet need (frequent users of health care, households with low incomes and children and older people who are not already exempt); regularly monitoring user charges revenue and disaggregating data by type of care and exempt categories; abolishing the use of balance billing; harmonizing user charges policy across the country; and keeping primary care free at the point of use. A longer-term objective could include replacing percentage co-payments with low, fixed co-payments.

recommendations.title: Reduce provider dependence on informal payments.
recommendations.text: This can be achieved using a multi-pronged approach to collect data on the magnitude of informal payments and their root causes; raise awareness among the population regarding their entitlements, so that people do not pay more than they should for covered care; improve the design of the benefits package (Decree 600); strengthen health care purchasing arrangements; and increase public spending on health.

recommendations.title: Increase public spending on health, particularly for primary care.
recommendations.text: Public spending on health has not kept pace with gross domestic product. The Government should increase the share of the budget allocated to health and find ways to monitor and increase spending on primary care, including on a wider range of diagnostic tests and outpatient prescribed medicines for the whole population.

recommendations.title: Improve the pooling and allocation of public resources and strengthen purchasing arrangements.
recommendations.text: Pool funds at regional rather than district level to pave the way for mechanisms to allocate resources based on population health needs. Strengthen primary care purchasing by improving capitation-based contracting to enable needs-based allocation of resources to providers.

recommendations.title: Safeguard population coverage by continuing to base entitlement on residence or citizenship when mandatory health insurance is introduced.
recommendations.text: Entitlement is based on citizenship and nearly the whole population is covered (a strong feature of the health system). One proposal in the 2008 health insurance law (whose implementation has been postponed several times) is to link entitlement to the payment of new mandatory health insurance contributions, which would erode population coverage. International experience shows that it is possible to set up a mandatory health insurance scheme without introducing a link between entitlement and payment of contributions. The Government should also consider expanding entitlement to at least some publicly financed health care for refugees without disabilities and undocumented migrants, in line with international standards.

recommendations.title: Monitor patterns of use and unmet need for key types of care, including outpatient medicines.

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: People who do not have any formal identification may face barriers to registering with a family doctor, which is a requirement for access to publicly financed health care. While refugees are entitled to the same health services as citizens, asylum seekers and undocumented migrants are entitled to emergency care only and must pay the full cost after treatment.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: Coverage of medicines, medical products and dental care is limited. The list of covered outpatient medicines (Affordable Medicines Program) is expanding but does not cover many essential medicines. The list of covered inpatient medicines (the Ukrainian Essential Medicines List) is also small and access is further limited by budget constraints and inefficiencies in procuring and distributing medicines. Adults only have access to emergency dental care. Informal payments are widespread, particularly in hospitals.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: User charges are limited to outpatient prescribed medicines. The range of covered medicines is small, however, and people frequently pay out of pocket, even for covered services, due to underfunding and other inefficiencies.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI mainly plays a supplementary role, providing faster access to treatment and greater choice of provider. It covers around 3% of the population and accounted for 2% of current spending on health in 2021. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

recommendations.title: Prioritize public spending on comprehensive primary care, which includes funding for better access to medicines and diagnostic tests, and strengthen the prescribing, dispensing, price regulation and availability of medicines
recommendations.text:
Continue to expand the Affordable Medicines Program (AMP), so that it better meets the health needs of the population, and ensure that the medicines it covers are cost-effective, aligned with clinical guidelines and target the needs of households with low incomes.

Develop incentives and other mechanisms to stimulate INN prescribing by doctors and the dispensing of cheaper medicines by pharmacies, and monitor prescribing and dispensing under the AMP. Ensure an equitable distribution of pharmacies participating in the AMP across oblasts. 

Expand the UEML and monitor spending on inpatient medicines. This should be accompanied by rules to prevent providers from asking people to pay for medicines covered by the UEML and by the monitoring of providers.

recommendations.title: Reduce informal payments for inpatient care
recommendations.text:
Curb ‘charitable donations’ through better enforcement of the provider-purchaser contract provisions that already prohibit these charges and by monitoring providers. Ensure that health care providers do not induce the use of services on the negative list and that there is no double billing of covered services.

Develop a comprehensive and long-term strategy to tackle the root causes of informal payments and implement strategies to improve people’s understanding of their health care entitlements.

recommendations.title: Improve the process for reviewing the Program of Medical Guarantees
recommendations.text: The process for defining the publicly financed benefits package should be more explicit, transparent and inclusive of a range of perspectives.

recommendations.title: Strengthen the capacity of the National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU) to be an active purchaser of services, which will allow it to make better use of public resources
Enhance protection for households with low incomes and others at high risk of catastrophic health spending
recommendations.text: The Government will need to continue to give priority to health in allocating public spending. It should also support the NHSU so that it is better able to reduce out-of-pocket payments for the services that cause financial hardship and to account for changing health needs in the context of the war and growing poverty.

gaps.title: Main gaps in population coverage
gaps.text: Emergency care, primary care and a range of community health services are available free of charge for everyone living in the UK, regardless of residence status. But some people with irregular or insecure immigration status can face barriers to access if they are asked to provide ID or proof of address when registering with a National Health Service (NHS) provider and are incorrectly denied registration. When it comes to hospital care, overseas visitors may be required to pay for treatment, but there are exemptions for certain groups of people, like asylum seekers and refugees. However, a survey of members of the British Medical Association found that 55% of doctors working with refugees and asylum seekers were frequently or sometimes uncertain about their entitlements, which can pose a barrier to access.

gaps.title: Main gaps in service coverage
gaps.text: The National Health Service does not cover eye care (glasses, contact lenses) for working-age adults, unless they have a low income or certain chronic conditions. It covers dental care, but the supply of dental practices offering publicly financed treatment is limited: in 2019/20 more than half of all adults had not seen a dentist within the previous 24 months (as is recommended) and more than two in five children had not had an appointment in the previous 12 months. Substantial waiting times for planned hospital care is also an issue and waiting times tend to be significantly longer in more deprived areas.

gaps.title: Main gaps caused by user charges
gaps.text: Most adults in the UK are required to pay user charges for dental care and eye care (glasses and contact lenses). Adults are also required to pay for outpatient prescriptions in England, but there are exemptions for people aged > 59, people with low incomes and people with selected chronic conditions; this means about 90% of prescriptions are provided without charge.

gaps.title: VHI role in filling gaps in coverage
gaps.text: VHI (commonly known as private medical insurance in the UK) mainly plays a supplementary role, providing access to private providers (e.g. private hospitals and specialists and private wards of NHS hospitals) and faster access to diagnostic tests and treatment. It can also be used to obtain services not well covered by the National Health Service (e.g. dental care), including some that are considered low value, but this depends on each VHI policy and does not apply to experimental tests or treatment. In 2022 it accounted for 2.5% of current spending on health. Expanding VHI is likely to increase inequality in access to health care.

notes.Indicator_HS_Breakdown_Spending:
Data are based on the System of Health Accounts (SHA) classification.

Public spending on health refers here to all compulsory health financing schemes (SHA code HF 1), including compulsory private health insurance (HF 1.2.2) in France, Germany, Netherlands (Kingdom of the) and Switzerland.

Voluntary health insurance (HF 2.1) includes government subsidies for voluntary health insurance in Croatia, Georgia and Portugal.

Out-of-pocket payments (HF 3).

In columns that do not sum to 100%, the spending that is not shown may correspond to non-profit institutions serving households (including development agencies) (HF 2.2), enterprise financing schemes (HF 2.3) and unspecified voluntary health care payment schemes (HF 2.nec).

Dental care: ‘dental outpatient curative care’ (HC 1.3.2).

Diagnostic tests: ‘ancillary services (not specified by function)’ (HC 4) – ‘patient transportation’ (HC 4.3). The EU average for diagnostic tests excludes Denmark, Italy and Portugal as these countries do not report patient transport separately from ancillary services.

Inpatient care: ‘inpatient curative care’ (HC 1.1) + inpatient rehabilitative care (HC 2.1).

Medicines: ‘pharmaceuticals and other medical durable goods’ (HC 5.1).

Medical products: ‘therapeutic appliances and other medical goods’ (HC 5.2).

Outpatient care: ‘outpatient curative care’ (HC 1.3) + outpatient rehabilitative care’ (HC 2.3) – ‘dental outpatient curative care (HC 1.3.2). The EU average for outpatient care excludes Italy and Portugal as these countries do not report dental care separately from other types of outpatient care.
